title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
author: Leo Tolstoy
translator: a new translation made for this app from the Russian original

body: In the big building of the law courts, during a break in the hearing of the Melvinsky case, the members of the court and the public prosecutor met in Ivan Yegorovich Shebek’s office, and the conversation turned to the famous Krasov case. Fyodor Vasilyevich grew heated, arguing that it was outside the court’s jurisdiction; Ivan Yegorovich held his ground; while Pyotr Ivanovich, who had not joined the argument at the start, took no part in it and was looking through the *Gazette*, which had just been brought in.
“Gentlemen!” he said. “Ivan Ilyich has died.”
“Really?”
“Here, read it,” he said to Fyodor Vasilyevich, handing him the fresh issue, still smelling of ink.

Inside a black border was printed: “Praskovya Fyodorovna Golovina, with deep sorrow, informs relatives and friends of the death of her beloved husband, Ivan Ilyich Golovin, Member of the Court of Justice, which took place on the 4th of February of this year 1882. The funeral will be on Friday at one o’clock in the afternoon.”

Ivan Ilyich had been a colleague of the gentlemen gathered there, and they had all liked him. He had been ill for several weeks; it was said his illness was incurable. His post had been kept for him, but there had been talk that, in the event of his death, Alekseyev might be appointed to his place, and to Alekseyev’s place either Vinnikov or Shtabel. So that on hearing of Ivan Ilyich’s death, the first thought of each of the gentlemen in the office was what this death might mean for the transfers or promotions of the members themselves or their acquaintances.

“Now I’m sure to get Shtabel’s post, or Vinnikov’s,” thought Fyodor Vasilyevich. “It was promised me long ago, and the promotion means eight hundred roubles more a year for me, not counting the allowance for the office.”
“Now I must ask for my brother-in-law to be transferred from Kaluga,” thought Pyotr Ivanovich. “My wife will be very pleased. Now she won’t be able to say I’ve never done anything for her family.”
“I thought he would never get up again,” Pyotr Ivanovich said aloud. “It’s a pity.”
“But what exactly was wrong with him?”
“The doctors couldn’t decide. That is, they decided, but differently. When I saw him last, I thought he would get better.”
“And I never went to see him after the holidays. I kept meaning to.”
“Did he have any money?”
“I think his wife has something very small. But a trifle.”
“Yes, we must go. They lived terribly far away.”
“Far from you, you mean. Everything is far from you.”
“He can never forgive me for living across the river,” said Pyotr Ivanovich, smiling at Shebek. And they talked about the great distances in the city, and went back into the court.

Apart from the thoughts about transfers and possible changes at work that this death set off in each of them, the very fact of the death of a close acquaintance aroused in all who heard of it, as always, a feeling of gladness that it was he who had died and not I.

“Well, he’s dead; but I’m not,” each of them thought or felt. And his close acquaintances, Ivan Ilyich’s so-called friends, could not help thinking too that they would now have to carry out the very tedious duties of decency: go to the funeral service and pay the widow a visit of condolence.
The closest of all were Fyodor Vasilyevich and Pyotr Ivanovich.
Pyotr Ivanovich had been at the School of Law with Ivan Ilyich and considered himself indebted to him.

Having told his wife at dinner the news of Ivan Ilyich’s death and his thoughts about the possibility of getting his brother-in-law transferred to their district, Pyotr Ivanovich did not lie down for his usual rest, but put on his tailcoat and drove to Ivan Ilyich’s.

At the entrance to Ivan Ilyich’s flat stood a carriage and two cabs. Downstairs in the hall, by the coat stand, the lid of the coffin, covered in gold brocade, with tassels and braid polished with powder, was leaning against the wall. Two ladies in black were taking off their fur coats. One, Ivan Ilyich’s sister, he knew; the other lady he did not. Pyotr Ivanovich’s colleague Schwartz was coming downstairs and, seeing him come in from the top step, stopped and winked at him, as if to say: “Ivan Ilyich has made a mess of things; not like you and me.”

Schwartz’s face with its English side-whiskers, and his whole lean figure in a tailcoat, had, as always, an elegant solemnity, and this solemnity, which always contradicted Schwartz’s playful character, had a special piquancy here. So Pyotr Ivanovich thought.

Pyotr Ivanovich let the ladies go ahead of him and slowly followed them up the stairs. Schwartz did not come down but stopped at the top. Pyotr Ivanovich understood why: he obviously wanted to arrange where they would play cards that evening. The ladies went up the stairs to the widow, while Schwartz, his strong lips seriously pressed together and a playful look in his eyes, pointed Pyotr Ivanovich with a movement of his eyebrows to the right, to the dead man’s room.

Pyotr Ivanovich went in, as always happens, uncertain what he would have to do there. One thing he knew: in such cases crossing yourself never hurts. As to whether one ought also to bow, he was not quite sure, and so he chose the middle course: on entering the room he began to cross himself and, as it were, to bow slightly. As far as the movements of his hands and head allowed, he looked around the room at the same time. Two young men, one a schoolboy, nephews probably, were crossing themselves as they left the room. An old woman stood motionless. And a lady with strangely raised eyebrows was saying something to her in a whisper. A church reader in a frock coat, brisk and resolute, was reading something aloud in a tone that excluded all contradiction. The servant Gerasim, passing in front of Pyotr Ivanovich with light steps, was sprinkling something on the floor. Seeing this, Pyotr Ivanovich at once caught a faint smell of a decomposing body. On his last visit to Ivan Ilyich, Pyotr Ivanovich had seen this peasant in the study; he had been acting as a nurse, and Ivan Ilyich had been particularly fond of him. Pyotr Ivanovich kept crossing himself and bowing slightly in a direction halfway between the coffin, the reader and the icons on the table in the corner. Then, when this movement of crossing himself began to seem to him to have gone on too long, he stopped and began to look at the dead man.

The dead man lay, as dead men always lie, especially heavily, in a dead man’s way, his stiffened limbs sunk into the lining of the coffin, his head bent forever on the pillow, and he displayed, as dead men always do, his yellow, waxen forehead with bald patches on the sunken temples, and his protruding nose, which seemed to press down on his upper lip. He had changed a great deal, and grown even thinner since Pyotr Ivanovich had last seen him, but, as with all dead men, his face was more handsome, and above all more significant, than it had been when he was alive. On the face was an expression that what had needed to be done had been done, and done rightly. Besides this, there was in the expression a reproach, or a reminder, to the living. This reminder seemed to Pyotr Ivanovich out of place, or at least not to concern him. Something felt unpleasant to him, and so Pyotr Ivanovich hastily crossed himself once more and, too hastily as it seemed to him, not quite in keeping with decency, turned and went to the door. Schwartz was waiting for him in the next room, his legs planted wide apart and both hands behind his back playing with his top hat. One look at Schwartz’s playful, well-groomed and elegant figure refreshed Pyotr Ivanovich. Pyotr Ivanovich understood that he, Schwartz, was above all this and did not give in to depressing impressions. His very appearance said: the incident of Ivan Ilyich’s funeral service cannot possibly be considered sufficient grounds for declaring the order of the session disrupted; that is, nothing can prevent us from breaking open a new pack of cards with a snap this very evening, while the footman sets out four fresh candles; in general there is no reason to suppose that this incident could stop us spending a pleasant evening today as well. And he said so in a whisper to Pyotr Ivanovich as he passed, proposing that they meet for a game at Fyodor Vasilyevich’s. But it was evidently not Pyotr Ivanovich’s fate to play cards that evening. Praskovya Fyodorovna, a short, fat woman who, in spite of all her efforts to the contrary, still widened from the shoulders downwards, all in black, her head covered with lace and with the same strangely raised eyebrows as the lady standing by the coffin, came out of her rooms with some other ladies and, showing them to the door of the dead man’s room, said:
“The service will begin in a moment; please go in.”

Schwartz, bowing vaguely, stood still, evidently neither accepting nor declining the invitation. Praskovya Fyodorovna, recognising Pyotr Ivanovich, sighed, came right up to him, took his hand and said:
“I know you were a true friend of Ivan Ilyich’s...” and looked at him, waiting for him to act in a way that matched these words.

Pyotr Ivanovich knew that just as in there one had to cross oneself, here one had to press her hand, sigh and say, “Believe me!” And so he did. And having done it, he felt that the desired result had been achieved: that he was touched and she was touched.
“Come, before it begins in there; I need to talk to you,” said the widow. “Give me your arm.”

Pyotr Ivanovich gave her his arm, and they went towards the inner rooms, past Schwartz, who winked sadly at Pyotr Ivanovich: “So much for our cards! Don’t hold it against us if we find another partner. Perhaps you can make a fifth, when you get away,” said his playful look.

Pyotr Ivanovich sighed still more deeply and sadly, and Praskovya Fyodorovna gratefully pressed his arm. Going into her drawing room, upholstered in pink cretonne and lit by a dim lamp, they sat down at the table: she on the sofa, and Pyotr Ivanovich on a low pouffe whose springs had gone and which gave way unevenly under him. Praskovya Fyodorovna had meant to warn him to sit on another chair, but decided that such a warning did not suit her position, and changed her mind. As he sat down on this pouffe, Pyotr Ivanovich remembered how Ivan Ilyich had furnished this drawing room and had consulted him about this very pink cretonne with green leaves. Going past the table to sit on the sofa (the whole drawing room was crammed with knick-knacks and furniture), the widow caught the black lace of her black shawl on the carving of the table. Pyotr Ivanovich half rose to free it, and the pouffe, released, began to heave and push him. The widow began to free her lace herself, and Pyotr Ivanovich sat down again, crushing the pouffe rebelling beneath him. But the widow had not freed it all, and Pyotr Ivanovich rose again, and again the pouffe rebelled and even creaked. When all this was over, she took out a clean cambric handkerchief and began to weep. But the episode with the lace and the struggle with the pouffe had cooled Pyotr Ivanovich, and he sat frowning. This awkward situation was broken by Sokolov, Ivan Ilyich’s butler, who came to report that the plot in the cemetery that Praskovya Fyodorovna had chosen would cost two hundred roubles. She stopped weeping and, looking at Pyotr Ivanovich with the air of a victim, said in French that it was very hard for her. Pyotr Ivanovich made a silent sign expressing his complete conviction that it could not be otherwise.

“Please do smoke,” she said in a voice that was at once generous and crushed, and turned to discussing with Sokolov the price of the plot. Lighting his cigarette, Pyotr Ivanovich heard her ask in great detail about the various prices of the ground and settle on the one she would take. Besides that, when she had finished with the plot, she gave orders about the choir. Sokolov left.

“I do everything myself,” she said to Pyotr Ivanovich, moving the albums on the table to one side; and, noticing that his ash was threatening the table, she promptly pushed an ashtray towards him and said: “I think it is pretence to claim that grief prevents one from attending to practical matters. On the contrary, if anything can... not console me, but distract me, it is looking after things for him.” She took out her handkerchief again, as if about to weep, and suddenly, as if mastering herself, shook herself and began to speak calmly:
“But I have some business with you.”
Pyotr Ivanovich bowed, not allowing the springs of the pouffe, which at once began to stir under him, to get out of hand.
“In the last days he suffered terribly.”
“Did he suffer very much?” asked Pyotr Ivanovich.

“Oh, terribly! For the last hours, not minutes, hours, he screamed without stopping. For three days and nights on end he screamed without pausing for breath. It was unbearable. I cannot understand how I bore it; you could hear it through three doors. Oh, what I have been through!”
“And was he really conscious?” asked Pyotr Ivanovich.
“Yes,” she whispered, “to the last minute. He said goodbye to us a quarter of an hour before he died, and he asked us to take Volodya away.”

The thought of the suffering of a man he had known so closely, first as a cheerful boy, a schoolboy, then as a grown-up partner at cards, in spite of the unpleasant awareness of his own pretence and this woman’s, suddenly horrified Pyotr Ivanovich. He saw again that forehead, that nose pressing down on the lip, and he felt afraid for himself.

“Three days and nights of terrible suffering, and death. Why, that could come for me too, at once, at any minute,” he thought, and for a moment he was afraid. But at once, he did not know how, the usual thought came to his rescue: that this had happened to Ivan Ilyich and not to him, that it ought not to and could not happen to him; that by thinking like this he was giving in to a gloomy mood, which one ought not to do, as was evident from Schwartz’s face. And having reasoned like this, Pyotr Ivanovich calmed down and began to ask with interest about the details of Ivan Ilyich’s end, as if death were an adventure peculiar to Ivan Ilyich and not at all peculiar to himself.

After various conversations about the details of the truly terrible physical sufferings that Ivan Ilyich had endured (details that Pyotr Ivanovich learned only from the way Ivan Ilyich’s torments had affected Praskovya Fyodorovna’s nerves), the widow evidently found it necessary to get down to business.
“Oh, Pyotr Ivanovich, how hard it is, how terribly hard, how terribly hard,” and she began to weep again.
Pyotr Ivanovich sighed and waited for her to blow her nose. When she had blown her nose, he said:

“Believe me...” and again she began to talk and told him what was evidently her chief business with him; and this business consisted of questions about how, on the occasion of her husband’s death, she could get money from the government. She pretended to ask Pyotr Ivanovich’s advice about a pension; but he saw that she already knew, down to the smallest details, things he did not know himself: everything that could be got out of the government on the occasion of this death; and that what she wanted to find out was whether some way could be found of getting still more money. Pyotr Ivanovich tried to think of such a way, but after thinking a little and, for decency’s sake, abusing our government for its stinginess, he said he thought nothing more could be got. Then she sighed and evidently began to think of a way to get rid of her visitor. He understood this, put out his cigarette, stood up, pressed her hand and went out into the hall.

In the dining room with the clock that Ivan Ilyich had been so pleased to find in an antique shop, Pyotr Ivanovich met the priest and several more acquaintances who had come for the service, and saw Ivan Ilyich’s daughter, a pretty young woman he knew. She was all in black. Her very slender waist seemed slenderer still. She had a gloomy, determined, almost angry look. She bowed to Pyotr Ivanovich as if he were somehow to blame. Behind the daughter, with the same offended look, stood a rich young man Pyotr Ivanovich knew, an examining magistrate, her fiancé, as he had heard. He bowed to them dejectedly and was about to go into the dead man’s room when from under the stairs appeared the little figure of the son, a schoolboy, terribly like Ivan Ilyich. He was the little Ivan Ilyich whom Pyotr Ivanovich remembered from the School of Law. His eyes were tear-stained, and also the kind of eyes impure boys of thirteen or fourteen have. Seeing Pyotr Ivanovich, the boy began to frown, sternly and shamefacedly. Pyotr Ivanovich nodded to him and went into the dead man’s room. The service began: candles, groans, incense, tears, sobs. Pyotr Ivanovich stood frowning, looking at the feet in front of him. He did not once look at the dead man, did not give in to the weakening influences to the very end, and was one of the first to leave. There was nobody in the hall. Gerasim, the servant, darted out of the dead man’s room, tossed all the fur coats about with his strong hands to find Pyotr Ivanovich’s, and handed it to him.
“Well, Gerasim, my friend?” said Pyotr Ivanovich, to say something. “It’s sad, isn’t it?”

“It’s God’s will. We shall all come to it,” said Gerasim, showing his white, even, peasant’s teeth, and, like a man in the thick of hard work, he briskly opened the door, called the coachman, helped Pyotr Ivanovich in, and sprang back to the porch, as if wondering what else he could do.
It was especially pleasant for Pyotr Ivanovich to breathe the clean air after the smell of incense, the corpse and carbolic acid.
“Where to, sir?” asked the coachman.
“It isn’t late. I’ll call on Fyodor Vasilyevich after all.”
And Pyotr Ivanovich drove there. And indeed he found them finishing the first rubber, so that it was convenient for him to come in as a fifth.
## II
The past history of Ivan Ilyich’s life was most simple and ordinary, and most terrible.

Ivan Ilyich died at forty-five, a Member of the Court of Justice. He was the son of an official who had made, in various ministries and departments in Petersburg, the kind of career that brings people to a position in which, although it becomes clear that they are unfit to perform any real duties, they still cannot be dismissed because of their long past service and their rank; and so they receive invented, fictitious posts and non-fictitious thousands, from six to ten thousand a year, on which they live on into deep old age.
Such was the Privy Councillor Ilya Yefimovich Golovin, a useless member of various useless institutions.

He had three sons, and Ivan Ilyich was the second. The eldest was making the same kind of career as his father, only in another ministry, and was already nearing the stage of service at which that inertia of salary is reached. The third son was a failure. He had spoiled things for himself everywhere and was now serving on the railways; his father, his brothers, and especially their wives, not only disliked meeting him but, unless it was absolutely necessary, did not even remember that he existed. Their sister was married to Baron Greff, the same kind of Petersburg official as his father-in-law. Ivan Ilyich was *le phénix de la famille*, the pride of the family, as people said. He was not as cold and correct as the eldest, nor as reckless as the youngest. He was halfway between them: an intelligent, lively, pleasant and decent man. He was educated at the School of Law together with his younger brother. The younger brother did not finish and was expelled in the fifth year, but Ivan Ilyich completed the course with credit. Already at the School of Law he was what he remained for the rest of his life: a capable man, cheerfully good-natured and sociable, but strict in carrying out what he considered his duty; and he considered his duty to be everything that was considered so by those in the highest positions. He was not a toady, either as a boy or later as a grown man, but from his earliest years he was drawn, like a fly to the light, to the people in the highest positions in society; he took on their manners and their views of life, and established friendly relations with them. All the enthusiasms of his childhood and youth passed without leaving much trace; he gave himself up to sensuality and to vanity and, towards the end, in the senior classes, to liberalism, but always within certain limits, which his instinct pointed out to him correctly.

At the School of Law he had done things which had earlier seemed to him great vileness and which had made him disgusted with himself while he was doing them; but later, seeing that such things were done by people of high standing too and were not considered bad by them, he did not exactly come to think them good, but forgot them entirely, and was not in the least troubled by the memory of them.

Having left the School of Law with the tenth rank, and having received money from his father for his outfit, Ivan Ilyich ordered his clothes from Scharmer, the fashionable tailor, hung on his watch chain a medallion inscribed *respice finem*, “consider the end”, said goodbye to the prince who was patron of the school and to his tutor, dined with his friends at Donon’s, and, with a new fashionable trunk, linen, clothes, shaving and toilet things and a travelling rug, all ordered and bought in the very best shops, he left for the provinces to take up the post of secretary for special commissions to the governor, which his father had found for him.

In the provinces Ivan Ilyich at once made for himself the same easy and pleasant position he had had at the School of Law. He worked, made his career, and at the same time amused himself pleasantly and decently; now and then he travelled to the districts on his superiors’ instructions, carried himself with dignity towards both those above and those below him, and carried out the tasks given him, mainly concerning the religious dissenters, with an exactness and incorruptible honesty of which he could not help being proud.

In official matters, in spite of his youth and his taste for light amusement, he was extremely reserved, formal and even stern; but in society he was often playful and witty, and always good-natured, decent and *bon enfant*, a good fellow, as his chief and his chief’s wife said of him; he was like one of the family in their house.

In the provinces there was also an affair with one of the ladies who threw herself at the smart young lawyer; there was a milliner; there were drinking parties with visiting aides-de-camp and trips after supper to a certain street on the edge of town; there was also some currying favour with his chief and even with his chief’s wife; but all this bore such a high tone of decency that it could not be called by bad names: it all came only under the heading of the French saying, *il faut que jeunesse se passe*, youth must have its fling. Everything was done with clean hands, in clean shirts, with French words, and above all in the very highest society, and therefore with the approval of people of high standing.
Ivan Ilyich served like this for five years, and then came a change in his career. The new judicial institutions appeared; new men were needed.
And Ivan Ilyich became that new man.

Ivan Ilyich was offered the post of examining magistrate, and he accepted it, even though the post was in another province and he would have to abandon the relations he had established and establish new ones. His friends saw him off, had a group photograph taken, presented him with a silver cigarette case, and he left for his new post.

As an examining magistrate Ivan Ilyich was just as *comme il faut*, decent, able to separate his official duties from his private life, and commanding general respect, as he had been as secretary for special commissions. The work of an examining magistrate itself was far more interesting and attractive to Ivan Ilyich than his earlier work. In his earlier post it had been pleasant to walk with a free stride, in his Scharmer uniform, past the trembling petitioners waiting to be received and the officials who envied him, straight into his chief’s office, and sit down with him to tea and a cigarette; but there had been few people directly dependent on his will. Such people were only the district police chiefs and the dissenters, when he was sent on commissions; and he liked to treat such people, who depended on him, courteously, almost as comrades; he liked to let them feel that here he was, who could crush them, treating them simply and in a friendly way. There were few such people then. But now, as an examining magistrate, Ivan Ilyich felt that everyone, everyone without exception, the most important and self-satisfied people, were all in his hands, and that he had only to write certain words on a sheet of headed paper, and this important, self-satisfied person would be brought to him as an accused man or a witness, and would, if he did not choose to have him seated, stand before him and answer his questions. Ivan Ilyich never abused this power of his; on the contrary, he tried to soften its expression; but the awareness of this power, and the possibility of softening it, were for him the chief interest and attraction of his new work. In the work itself, in the investigations, Ivan Ilyich very quickly mastered the technique of setting aside all circumstances that did not concern the case, and of putting even the most complicated case into a form in which it appeared on paper only in its external aspect, in which his personal view was completely excluded, and, above all, in which all the required formalities were observed. This work was new. And he was one of the first men to work out in practice how to apply the legal statutes of 1864.

On moving to the new town as examining magistrate, Ivan Ilyich made new acquaintances and connections, set himself up in a new way and adopted a somewhat different tone. He placed himself at a certain dignified distance from the provincial authorities, chose the best circle among the lawyers and the rich gentry living in the town, and adopted a tone of mild dissatisfaction with the government, moderate liberalism and civilised public spirit. At the same time, without changing the elegance of his dress in the least, Ivan Ilyich in his new post stopped shaving his chin and let his beard grow where it pleased.

Ivan Ilyich’s life in the new town also turned out very pleasant: the society that took a stand against the governor was friendly and good; his salary was larger; and no small pleasure was added to life by whist, which Ivan Ilyich now began to play, having a gift for playing cards cheerfully, thinking quickly and very subtly, so that on the whole he always came out ahead.

After two years of service in the new town, Ivan Ilyich met his future wife. Praskovya Fyodorovna Mikhel was the most attractive, intelligent and brilliant girl in the circle in which Ivan Ilyich moved. Among the other amusements and relaxations from his work as a magistrate, Ivan Ilyich established a playful, light relationship with Praskovya Fyodorovna.

When he was secretary for special commissions, Ivan Ilyich had danced as a rule; as an examining magistrate he danced only as an exception. He danced now in the spirit of: “Although I serve in the new institutions and in the fifth class, when it comes to dancing I can prove that in this field too I can do better than others.” So now and then, at the end of an evening, he danced with Praskovya Fyodorovna, and it was mainly during these dances that he won her. She fell in love with him. Ivan Ilyich had no clear, definite intention of marrying, but when the girl fell in love with him, he put the question to himself: “Really, why not marry?” he said to himself.

Miss Praskovya Fyodorovna came of a good noble family and was not bad-looking; there was a little money. Ivan Ilyich could have counted on a more brilliant match, but this too was a good match. Ivan Ilyich had his salary; she, he hoped, would bring as much again. Good connections; and she was a sweet, pretty and thoroughly decent woman. To say that Ivan Ilyich married because he fell in love with his bride and found in her sympathy for his views of life would be as unjust as to say that he married because the people in his circle approved of the match. Ivan Ilyich married for both reasons: he was doing something pleasant for himself in acquiring such a wife, and at the same time he was doing what people in the highest positions considered right.
And Ivan Ilyich married.

The process of marrying itself, and the first period of married life, with conjugal caresses, new furniture, new crockery, new linen, went very well until his wife became pregnant, so that Ivan Ilyich was already beginning to think that marriage would not only not disturb the character of life that was easy, pleasant, cheerful, always decent and approved by society, which Ivan Ilyich considered natural to life in general, but would even enhance it. But then, from the first months of his wife’s pregnancy, something new appeared, something unexpected, unpleasant, heavy and indecent, which could not have been expected and which there was no way of getting rid of.

His wife, without any reason, as it seemed to Ivan Ilyich, *de gaieté de cœur*, out of sheer caprice, as he said to himself, began to disturb the pleasantness and decency of life: she was jealous of him for no reason, demanded that he pay court to her, found fault with everything and made unpleasant and coarse scenes.

At first Ivan Ilyich hoped to free himself from the unpleasantness of this situation by the same easy and decent attitude to life that had saved him before. He tried to ignore his wife’s moods and went on living as before, easily and pleasantly: he invited friends to his house for a game of cards, and tried going off himself to the club or to friends. But once his wife began to abuse him in coarse words with such energy, and continued to abuse him so persistently every time he did not do as she demanded, evidently firmly resolved not to stop until he gave in, that is, until he stayed at home and moped as she did, that Ivan Ilyich was horrified. He understood that married life, at least with his wife, did not always further the pleasures and decencies of life, but on the contrary often disturbed them, and that it was therefore necessary to protect himself from these disturbances. And Ivan Ilyich began to look for the means to do so. His work was the one thing that impressed Praskovya Fyodorovna, and by means of his work and the duties arising from it, Ivan Ilyich began to struggle with his wife, fencing off his own independent world.

With the birth of a child, the attempts at nursing and the various failures in it, and the real and imaginary illnesses of the child and the mother, in which Ivan Ilyich was required to take part but of which he could understand nothing, his need to fence off a world for himself outside the family became still more pressing.

As his wife became more irritable and demanding, Ivan Ilyich moved the centre of gravity of his life more and more into his work. He began to love his work more and became more ambitious than he had been before.

Very soon, no more than a year after his marriage, Ivan Ilyich understood that married life, while offering certain comforts, was in essence a very complicated and difficult business, towards which, in order to do one’s duty, that is, to lead a decent life approved by society, one had to work out a definite attitude, just as one had towards one’s work.

And Ivan Ilyich worked out such an attitude to married life for himself. He required of family life only those comforts it could give him, of dinner at home, a housekeeper, a bed, and above all that decency of external forms which was determined by public opinion. For the rest, he looked for cheerful pleasantness, and if he found it he was very grateful; but if he met with resistance and grumbling, he at once withdrew into his separate, fenced-off world of work and found his pleasures there.

Ivan Ilyich was valued as a good official, and after three years he was made assistant public prosecutor. His new duties, their importance, the possibility of bringing anyone to trial and putting him in prison, the publicity of his speeches, the success Ivan Ilyich had in this work: all this drew him still more to his work.
Children came. His wife grew more and more querulous and bad-tempered, but the attitude to home life that Ivan Ilyich had worked out made him almost impervious to her grumbling.

After seven years of service in one town, Ivan Ilyich was transferred to the post of public prosecutor in another province. They moved; there was little money, and his wife did not like the place they moved to. Although the salary was larger than before, life was more expensive; besides, two of the children died, and so family life became still more unpleasant for Ivan Ilyich.

Praskovya Fyodorovna blamed her husband for every misfortune that happened in this new place. Most subjects of conversation between husband and wife, especially the children’s upbringing, led to questions on which there were memories of quarrels, and quarrels were ready to flare up at any minute. There remained only those rare periods of being in love that came over the couple, but they did not last long. They were little islands on which they landed for a time, but then they set out again on a sea of hidden hostility, which showed itself in their estrangement from each other. This estrangement might have grieved Ivan Ilyich if he had thought that it ought not to be so, but by now he considered this situation not only normal but the very aim of all his activity in the family. His aim consisted in freeing himself more and more from these unpleasantnesses and giving them a character of harmlessness and decency; and he achieved this by spending less and less time with his family, and when he was obliged to, he tried to safeguard his position by the presence of outsiders. But the main thing was that Ivan Ilyich had his work. The whole interest of life was concentrated for him in the world of work. And this interest absorbed him. The awareness of his power, of the possibility of ruining any man he wished to ruin; his importance, even external, when he entered the court and met his subordinates; his success with those above and below him; and, above all, his mastery in conducting cases, which he felt: all this gladdened him, and, together with conversations with his colleagues, dinners and whist, filled his life. So that on the whole Ivan Ilyich’s life went on as he considered it ought to go: pleasantly and decently.

So he lived another seven years. His elder daughter was already sixteen, another child had died, and there remained a boy at the grammar school, a subject of dispute. Ivan Ilyich wanted to send him to the School of Law, but Praskovya Fyodorovna, to spite him, sent him to the grammar school. The daughter was taught at home and was growing up well; the boy too was doing fairly well at his lessons.
## III

So Ivan Ilyich’s life went on for seventeen years after his marriage. He was already an experienced prosecutor who had turned down several transfers while waiting for a more desirable post, when unexpectedly an unpleasant circumstance occurred that almost destroyed the calm of his life. Ivan Ilyich was expecting the post of presiding judge in a university town, but somehow Goppe got ahead of him and obtained it. Ivan Ilyich became irritated, began to make reproaches, and quarrelled with Goppe and with his immediate superiors; they became cold towards him, and at the next appointment he was passed over again.

This was in 1880. That year was the hardest of Ivan Ilyich’s life. That year it turned out, on the one hand, that his salary was not enough to live on, and on the other, that everyone had forgotten him, and that what seemed to him the greatest and cruellest injustice towards him seemed to others a perfectly ordinary matter. Even his father did not consider it his duty to help him. He felt that everyone had abandoned him, regarding his position, with a salary of 3,500 roubles, as perfectly normal and even fortunate. He alone knew that, with the awareness of the injustices done to him, with his wife’s eternal nagging, and with the debts he had begun to run up by living beyond his means, he alone knew that his position was far from normal.
That summer, to ease his finances, he took leave and went with his wife to spend the summer in the country, at Praskovya Fyodorovna’s brother’s.

In the country, without his work, Ivan Ilyich for the first time felt not just boredom but an unbearable anguish, and decided that he could not go on living like this and that some decisive steps had to be taken.

After a sleepless night, which Ivan Ilyich spent pacing the terrace, he decided to go to Petersburg to make efforts on his own behalf and, to punish those who had failed to appreciate him, to transfer to another ministry.
The next day, in spite of all his wife’s and brother-in-law’s attempts to dissuade him, he left for Petersburg.

He went for one thing: to beg for a post with a salary of five thousand. He no longer cared about any particular ministry, political direction or kind of work. All he needed was a post, a post with five thousand, in the administration, in the banks, on the railways, in the Empress Maria’s charitable institutions, even in the customs, but it must be five thousand, and he must get out of the ministry where they had failed to appreciate him.

And this journey of Ivan Ilyich’s was crowned with amazing, unexpected success. At Kursk an acquaintance, F. S. Ilyin, got into the first-class carriage and told him of a fresh telegram received by the governor of Kursk: there was to be an upheaval in the ministry in a few days; Pyotr Ivanovich was to be replaced by Ivan Semyonovich.

The expected upheaval, besides its significance for Russia, had a special significance for Ivan Ilyich, because by bringing forward a new man, Pyotr Petrovich, and evidently his friend Zakhar Ivanovich, it was in the highest degree favourable to Ivan Ilyich. Zakhar Ivanovich was a colleague and friend of Ivan Ilyich’s.
In Moscow the news was confirmed. And on arriving in Petersburg Ivan Ilyich found Zakhar Ivanovich and received the promise of a sure post in his old Ministry of Justice.
A week later he telegraphed his wife:
“Zakhar in Miller’s place. I receive appointment at first report.”

Thanks to this change of personnel, Ivan Ilyich unexpectedly received an appointment in his old ministry which placed him two grades above his colleagues: five thousand in salary and three thousand five hundred for the expenses of moving. All his annoyance with his former enemies and with the whole ministry was forgotten, and Ivan Ilyich was completely happy.

Ivan Ilyich returned to the country cheerful and contented, as he had not been for a long time. Praskovya Fyodorovna cheered up too, and a truce was made between them. Ivan Ilyich told how everyone had honoured him in Petersburg, how all those who had been his enemies were put to shame and now fawned on him, how they envied him his position, and especially how much everyone in Petersburg loved him.

Praskovya Fyodorovna listened to this and pretended to believe it, and contradicted him in nothing, but only made plans for their new life in the town they were moving to. And Ivan Ilyich saw with joy that these plans were his plans, that they agreed, and that his life, which had stumbled, was once again taking on its true and natural character of cheerful pleasantness and decency.

Ivan Ilyich had come back only for a short time. On the 10th of September he had to take up his post, and besides, he needed time to settle into the new place, to move everything from the provinces, to buy and order a great many more things; in a word, to arrange things as they had been decided in his mind, and almost exactly as they had been decided in Praskovya Fyodorovna’s heart too.

And now, when everything had turned out so well, and when he and his wife agreed in their aims and, besides, spent little time together, they got on so well as they had not done since the first years of their married life. Ivan Ilyich had thought of taking his family with him at once, but the insistence of his sister-in-law and brother-in-law, who had suddenly become especially gracious and affectionate towards Ivan Ilyich and his family, meant that Ivan Ilyich left alone.

Ivan Ilyich left, and the cheerful state of mind produced by his success and by his harmony with his wife, each strengthening the other, did not leave him the whole time. He found a charming flat, exactly what husband and wife had dreamed of. Spacious, lofty reception rooms in the old style, a comfortable and magnificent study, rooms for his wife and daughter, a schoolroom for his son: all as if designed on purpose for them. Ivan Ilyich took charge of the furnishing himself, chose the wallpaper, bought furniture, especially antiques, to which he gave a particularly *comme il faut* style, and upholstery; and everything grew and grew and approached the ideal he had set himself. When he was halfway through, the result exceeded his expectations. He understood the *comme il faut*, elegant and not vulgar character that everything would take on when it was finished. Falling asleep, he pictured the reception room as it would be. Looking at the unfinished drawing room, he already saw the fireplace, the screen, the whatnot, and those little chairs scattered about, those dishes and plates on the walls, and the bronzes, when they were all in their places. He was delighted at the thought of how he would astonish Pasha and Lizanka, who also had taste in these things. They would never expect this. He had been particularly successful in finding and buying cheaply old things that gave everything an especially noble character. In his letters he deliberately made everything sound worse than it was, so as to astonish them. All this absorbed him so much that even his new work, though he loved it, absorbed him less than he had expected. During sessions of the court he had moments of absent-mindedness: he would be thinking about what kind of cornices to have for the curtains, straight or gathered. He was so taken up with it that he often did things himself, even moved the furniture and rehung the curtains himself. Once he climbed a ladder to show an upholsterer who did not understand how he wanted the curtains draped; he missed his footing and fell, but, being a strong and agile man, he caught himself, and only knocked his side against the handle of the window frame. The bruise hurt for a while, but soon passed. Ivan Ilyich felt especially cheerful and well all this time. He wrote: “I feel as if fifteen years had fallen off me.” He had expected to finish in September, but it dragged on until the middle of October. But it was charming: not only did he say so, but everyone who saw it told him so.

In reality it was just what is found among all people who are not quite rich, but who want to resemble the rich, and so only resemble one another: damask, ebony, flowers, carpets and bronzes, everything dark and gleaming, everything that all people of a certain kind do in order to resemble all people of a certain kind. And his was so like all the others that it could not even attract attention; but to him it all seemed something special. When he met his family at the railway station, brought them to his lit-up, finished flat, and a footman in a white tie opened the door into the hall decorated with flowers, and then they went into the drawing room and the study and gasped with pleasure, he was very happy, took them everywhere, drank in their praise and beamed with pleasure. That same evening, when Praskovya Fyodorovna asked him over tea, among other things, how he had fallen, he laughed and acted out how he had flown off the ladder and frightened the upholsterer.
“It’s not for nothing I’m an athlete. Anyone else would have been killed, but I only bumped myself here; it hurts when you touch it, but it’s passing already; it’s just a bruise.”

And they began to live in their new home, in which, as always happens once one has properly settled in, they lacked only one more room, and on their new income, which, as always, fell just a little short, some five hundred roubles; and it was very good. It was especially good at first, when not everything had been arranged and there was still arranging to do: something to buy, something to order, something to move, something to adjust. Although there were some disagreements between husband and wife, they were both so pleased and had so much to do that everything ended without big quarrels. When there was nothing left to arrange, it became a little boring and something seemed to be missing, but by then acquaintances had been made, habits formed, and life was full.

Ivan Ilyich, having spent the morning in court, came home to dinner, and at first his mood was good, although it suffered a little precisely because of the flat. (Every stain on the tablecloth or the damask, every broken curtain cord irritated him: he had put so much work into the furnishing that any damage pained him.) But in general Ivan Ilyich’s life went on as, by his creed, life ought to flow: easily, pleasantly and decently. He got up at nine, drank his coffee, read the newspaper, then put on his uniform and drove to the court. There the harness in which he worked had already been worn to shape; he slipped into it at once. Petitioners, inquiries at the office, the office itself, the sessions, public and administrative. In all this one had to know how to exclude everything raw and alive that always disturbs the regular course of official business: one must not admit any relations with people except official ones, and the reason for relations must be only official, and the relations themselves only official. For example, a man comes and wants to find out something. Ivan Ilyich, as a man not on duty, cannot have any relations with such a man; but if there is a relation to this man as to a member of the court, one that can be expressed on headed paper, then within the limits of that relation Ivan Ilyich does everything, absolutely everything, that can be done, and while doing so he keeps up the semblance of human, friendly relations, that is, politeness. As soon as the official relation ends, every other relation ends too. Ivan Ilyich possessed this skill of separating the official side, without mixing it with his real life, to the highest degree, and by long practice and talent he had developed it to such a degree that, like a virtuoso, he sometimes even allowed himself, as if in jest, to mix human and official relations. He allowed himself this because he felt he had the strength, whenever he needed to, to separate out the official part again and throw away the human. All this went on for Ivan Ilyich not only easily, pleasantly and decently, but even with virtuosity. In between he smoked, drank tea, talked a little about politics, a little about general affairs, a little about cards, and most of all about appointments. And tired, but with the feeling of a virtuoso who has played his part cleanly, one of the first violins in the orchestra, he came home. At home his daughter and her mother had gone out somewhere, or had someone visiting; his son was at school, or doing his lessons with tutors, diligently learning what is taught at school. Everything was good. After dinner, if there were no guests, Ivan Ilyich sometimes read a book that people were talking about, and in the evening sat down to work, that is, read papers, looked up the laws, compared statements and brought them under the laws. This was neither boring nor amusing to him. It was boring when he could have been playing cards; but if there was no game, it was still better than sitting alone or with his wife. Ivan Ilyich’s pleasures were little dinners, to which he invited ladies and gentlemen of social importance, and spending time with them in a way that resembled the usual way such people spend their time, just as his drawing room resembled all drawing rooms.

Once they even gave a party, with dancing. And Ivan Ilyich enjoyed himself, and everything went well, except that there was a big quarrel with his wife over the cakes and sweets: Praskovya Fyodorovna had her own plan, but Ivan Ilyich insisted on getting everything from an expensive confectioner, and ordered a great many cakes, and the quarrel was because cakes were left over and the confectioner’s bill came to forty-five roubles. The quarrel was big and unpleasant, so that Praskovya Fyodorovna said to him, “Fool, sourpuss!” And he clutched his head and in his anger said something about divorce. But the party itself was cheerful. The best society was there, and Ivan Ilyich danced with Princess Trufonova, the sister of the one known for founding the society “Bear My Sorrow Away”. The joys of his work were the joys of self-esteem; the joys of society were the joys of vanity; but Ivan Ilyich’s real joys were the joys of playing cards. He confessed that after everything, after any events at all, however joyless, in his life, the joy that burned like a candle before all the others was to sit down to a game of vint with good players and partners who did not shout, and it must be four (with five it was very painful to sit out, though you pretend you love it), and to play an intelligent, serious game (when the cards are running), then to have supper and drink a glass of wine. And after cards, especially when he had won a little (a lot was unpleasant), Ivan Ilyich went to bed in a particularly good mood.
So they lived. Their circle was made up of the very best people; important people came, and young people.

In their view of their circle of acquaintances, husband, wife and daughter were in complete agreement, and, without any discussion, they all alike edged away and freed themselves from all sorts of shabby friends and relatives who came flying in with endearments to the drawing room with Japanese plates on the walls. Soon these shabby friends stopped flying in, and only the very best society remained with the Golovins. Young men paid court to Lizanka, and Petrishchev, an examining magistrate, the son of Dmitry Ivanovich Petrishchev and the sole heir to his fortune, began to court Liza, so that Ivan Ilyich was already discussing with Praskovya Fyodorovna whether they should arrange a troika ride for them or get up some private theatricals. So they lived. And everything went on like this, without changing, and everything was very good.
## IV
They were all in good health. It could not be called ill health that Ivan Ilyich sometimes said he had a strange taste in his mouth and some discomfort in the left side of his abdomen.

But it happened that this discomfort began to increase and to turn, not yet into pain, but into a constant feeling of heaviness in his side and into a bad temper. This bad temper, growing stronger and stronger, began to spoil the pleasantness of easy and decent life that had been established in the Golovin family. Husband and wife began to quarrel more and more often, and soon the ease and pleasantness fell away, and decency alone was kept up with difficulty. Scenes became more frequent again. Again there remained only little islands, and few of them, on which husband and wife could meet without an explosion.

And Praskovya Fyodorovna now said, not without reason, that her husband had a difficult character. With her usual habit of exaggeration, she said he had always had this terrible character, and that it had taken her goodness to bear it for twenty years. It was true that the quarrels now started with him. His fault-finding always began just before dinner, and often just as he began to eat, over the soup. Now he would notice that some piece of crockery was damaged, now that the food was not right, now that his son had put his elbow on the table, now his daughter’s hair. And for everything he blamed Praskovya Fyodorovna. At first Praskovya Fyodorovna answered back and said unpleasant things to him, but twice at the start of dinner he flew into such a rage that she understood it was a morbid state brought on in him by taking food, and she controlled herself; she no longer answered back, but only hurried dinner along. Praskovya Fyodorovna counted her self-restraint a great merit. Having decided that her husband had a terrible character and had made her life a misery, she began to pity herself. And the more she pitied herself, the more she hated her husband. She began to wish he would die, but she could not wish it, because then there would be no salary. And this irritated her against him still more. She considered herself terribly unhappy precisely because even his death could not save her, and she was irritated, and hid it, and this hidden irritation of hers increased his irritation.

After one scene, in which Ivan Ilyich had been particularly unjust, and after which, when they talked it over, he said that he was indeed irritable but that it was because of his illness, she told him that if he was ill he must get treatment, and she demanded that he go to see a famous doctor.

He went. Everything was as he had expected; everything was done as it always is. The waiting, and the put-on, doctorly importance he knew so well, the very same importance he knew in himself in court; and the tapping, and the listening, and the questions requiring answers that were settled in advance and evidently unnecessary; and the significant air that suggested: just put yourself in our hands, and we shall arrange everything; we know, beyond doubt, how to arrange everything, in one and the same way for any person you like. It was all exactly the same as in court. Just as he in court put on an air before the accused, so the famous doctor now put on the same air before him.

The doctor said: this and that indicate that inside you there is this and that; but if this is not confirmed by examining this and that, then we must suppose that you have this and that. And if we suppose this, then... and so on. Only one question mattered to Ivan Ilyich: was his condition dangerous or not? But the doctor ignored this inappropriate question. From the doctor’s point of view, the question was idle and not open to discussion; all that existed was the weighing of probabilities: a floating kidney, chronic catarrh, or a disease of the appendix. There was no question of Ivan Ilyich’s life; there was a dispute between the floating kidney and the appendix. And before Ivan Ilyich’s eyes the doctor brilliantly settled this dispute in favour of the appendix, with the reservation that an analysis of the urine might provide new evidence, and that then the case would be reconsidered. All this was exactly what Ivan Ilyich himself had done a thousand times, in just as brilliant a manner, with the accused. The doctor summed up just as brilliantly, and looked triumphantly, even cheerfully, over his spectacles at the accused. From the doctor’s summing-up Ivan Ilyich drew the conclusion that things were bad, and that to the doctor, and perhaps to everyone, it did not matter, but that for him it was bad. And this conclusion struck Ivan Ilyich painfully, arousing in him a great pity for himself and great anger at this doctor, so indifferent to so important a question.
But he said nothing; he got up, put the money on the table and, with a sigh, said:
“We sick people probably often ask you inappropriate questions,” he said. “But in general, is this a dangerous illness or not?”

The doctor looked at him sternly with one eye through his spectacles, as if to say: “Prisoner, if you do not keep within the limits of the questions put to you, I shall be obliged to order your removal from the courtroom.”
“I have already told you what I considered necessary and appropriate,” said the doctor. “The tests will show the rest.” And the doctor bowed.

Ivan Ilyich went out slowly, got gloomily into his sledge and drove home. All the way he kept going over everything the doctor had said, trying to translate all those muddled, obscure scientific words into simple language and to read in them the answer to the question: is it bad, very bad for me, or is it still nothing much? And it seemed to him that the meaning of everything the doctor had said was that it was very bad. Everything in the streets seemed sad to Ivan Ilyich. The cabmen were sad, the houses were sad, the passers-by, the shops were sad. And this pain, this dull, gnawing pain that did not stop for a second, seemed, in connection with the doctor’s obscure words, to take on another, more serious meaning. Ivan Ilyich listened to it now with a new, heavy feeling.

He got home and began to tell his wife. His wife listened, but in the middle of his account their daughter came in with her hat on: she was about to go out with her mother. She made an effort and sat down to listen to this tedious talk, but she could not stand it for long, and her mother did not hear him out either.
“Well, I’m very glad,” said his wife. “So now, mind you take your medicine properly. Give me the prescription; I’ll send Gerasim to the chemist’s.” And she went to get dressed.
He held his breath while she was in the room, and sighed heavily when she went out.
“Well,” he said. “Perhaps it really is nothing yet.”

He began to take the medicines and follow the doctor’s instructions, which changed after the analysis of the urine. But just then it so happened that some confusion arose in this analysis and in what was to follow it. It was impossible to get through to the doctor himself, and it turned out that what was being done was not what the doctor had told him. Either the doctor had forgotten, or lied, or was hiding something from him.
But Ivan Ilyich all the same began to follow the instructions exactly, and in following them he found consolation for a while.

From the time of his visit to the doctor, Ivan Ilyich’s chief occupation became the exact carrying out of the doctor’s instructions about hygiene and taking medicine, and listening to his pain and to all the functions of his body. Ivan Ilyich’s chief interests became human illnesses and human health. When people spoke in his presence about the sick, about those who had died or recovered, especially from an illness that resembled his, he listened, trying to hide his agitation, asked questions, and applied what he heard to his own illness.

The pain did not lessen; but Ivan Ilyich made efforts to force himself to think he was better. And he could deceive himself as long as nothing upset him. But as soon as there was some unpleasantness with his wife, a setback at work, or bad cards at vint, he at once felt the full force of his illness. Before, he would have borne these setbacks, expecting that at any moment he would put things right, overcome them, wait for success, a grand slam. But now every setback cut him down and threw him into despair. He would say to himself: “Here I was just beginning to recover, and the medicine was already beginning to work, and now this damned misfortune or unpleasantness...” And he was angry at the misfortune, or at the people who were causing him unpleasantness and killing him, and he felt this anger killing him; but he could not restrain it. One would think it should have been clear to him that this anger at circumstances and people was making his illness worse, and that therefore he ought to pay no attention to unpleasant incidents; but he reasoned in exactly the opposite way: he said he needed peace, watched for everything that disturbed this peace, and at the slightest disturbance became irritated. His condition was made worse by his reading medical books and consulting doctors. The deterioration was so even that he could deceive himself by comparing one day with another: there was little difference. But when he consulted doctors, it seemed to him that he was getting worse, and even very quickly. And in spite of this he was constantly consulting doctors.

That month he went to another celebrity: the other celebrity said almost the same as the first, but put the questions differently. And the consultation with this celebrity only deepened Ivan Ilyich’s doubt and fear. A friend of a friend of his, a very good doctor, diagnosed the illness quite differently again, and although he promised recovery, with his questions and suppositions he confused Ivan Ilyich still more and increased his doubt. A homeopath diagnosed the illness differently again and gave him medicine, and Ivan Ilyich took it for about a week, secretly from everyone. But after a week, feeling no relief and losing confidence both in the earlier treatments and in this one, he sank into still greater dejection. Once a lady he knew told him about cures by icons. Ivan Ilyich caught himself listening attentively and checking whether the fact was true. This incident frightened him. “Have I really grown so weak in mind?” he said to himself. “Nonsense! It’s all rubbish; I mustn’t give in to nervousness, but choose one doctor and keep strictly to his treatment. That’s what I’ll do. Now it’s settled. I won’t think about it, and I’ll follow the treatment strictly until the summer. Then we shall see. Now an end to this wavering!” It was easy to say this, but impossible to carry out. The pain in his side kept wearing him down, seemed to keep growing stronger, became constant; the taste in his mouth became stranger and stranger; it seemed to him that his breath smelled of something disgusting; and his appetite and strength kept failing. He could not deceive himself: something terrible, new and so significant that nothing more significant had ever happened to Ivan Ilyich in his life was taking place inside him. And he alone knew about it; everyone around him did not understand, or did not want to understand, and thought that everything in the world was going on as before. It was this that tormented Ivan Ilyich more than anything. His household, above all his wife and daughter, who were in the full swing of going out into society, understood nothing, he saw; they were annoyed that he was so gloomy and demanding, as if he were to blame for it. Although they tried to hide it, he saw that he was a hindrance to them, and that his wife had worked out a certain attitude to his illness and kept to it regardless of what he said or did. The attitude was this:

“You know,” she would say to acquaintances, “Ivan Ilyich can’t follow his prescribed treatment strictly, the way sensible people do. One day he’ll take his drops and eat what he’s told and go to bed on time; the next day, if I don’t watch him, he’ll suddenly forget to take them, eat sturgeon (which he’s been forbidden) and sit up over cards until one in the morning.”
“Well, when was that?” Ivan Ilyich would say with annoyance. “Once, at Pyotr Ivanovich’s.”
“And yesterday with Shebek.”
“I couldn’t have slept anyway, with the pain...”
“Whatever the reason, you’ll never get well like this, and you torment us.”

Praskovya Fyodorovna’s outward attitude to her husband’s illness, which she expressed to others and to him, was that Ivan Ilyich was to blame for this illness and that the whole illness was a new unpleasantness he was causing his wife. Ivan Ilyich felt that this came out of her involuntarily, but that did not make it any easier for him.

At the court Ivan Ilyich noticed, or thought he noticed, the same strange attitude towards himself: now it seemed to him that people were watching him as a man who would soon be vacating his post; now his friends would suddenly begin to tease him in a friendly way about his nervousness, as if this awful, terrible, unheard-of thing that had taken root in him, that was ceaselessly sucking at him and irresistibly drawing him somewhere, were the most pleasant subject for a joke. Schwartz in particular irritated him, with his playfulness, his liveliness and his *comme il faut* manner, which reminded Ivan Ilyich of himself ten years before.

Friends would come to make up a game, and sit down. They dealt; the new cards were softened up; he sorted the diamonds together: seven of them. His partner said, “No trumps,” and supported him with two diamonds. What more could one want? It ought to be cheerful and lively: a grand slam. And suddenly Ivan Ilyich feels that sucking pain, that taste in his mouth, and it seems to him something wild that he can rejoice at a grand slam at the same time.

He looks at Mikhail Mikhailovich, his partner, at how he raps the table with his sanguine hand and politely and indulgently refrains from gathering up the tricks, but pushes them towards Ivan Ilyich so as to give him the pleasure of collecting them without having to trouble himself or stretch his arm far. “Does he think I’m so weak I can’t stretch my arm out?” thinks Ivan Ilyich; he forgets what are trumps, trumps his own partner’s card once too often, and loses the grand slam by three tricks; and what is most terrible of all is that he sees how Mikhail Mikhailovich suffers, and he does not care. And it is terrible to think why he does not care.

Everyone sees that he is having a hard time, and they say to him: “We can stop if you’re tired. Have a rest.” A rest? No, he isn’t tired at all; they finish the rubber. Everyone is gloomy and silent. Ivan Ilyich feels that he has brought this gloom upon them and cannot dispel it. They have supper and go home, and Ivan Ilyich is left alone with the awareness that his life is poisoned for him and poisons the lives of others, and that this poison is not weakening but penetrating his whole being more and more.

And with this awareness, and with physical pain as well, and with horror as well, he had to go to bed, and often lie awake from the pain for most of the night. And in the morning he had to get up again, dress, drive to the court, talk, write; or, if he did not go, be at home with the same twenty-four hours in the day, every one of which was torment. And he had to live like this on the edge of the abyss alone, without a single person who would understand him and pity him.

So a month went by, and two. Before the New Year his brother-in-law came to their town and stayed with them. Ivan Ilyich was at the court. Praskovya Fyodorovna had gone shopping. Going into his study, he found his brother-in-law there, a healthy, ruddy man, unpacking his suitcase himself. He raised his head at the sound of Ivan Ilyich’s steps and looked at him for a second in silence. That look revealed everything to Ivan Ilyich. His brother-in-law opened his mouth to gasp and stopped himself. That movement confirmed everything.
“Well, have I changed?”
“Yes... there is a change.”

And however much Ivan Ilyich steered the conversation afterwards towards his appearance, his brother-in-law said nothing. Praskovya Fyodorovna came home, and his brother-in-law went to her. Ivan Ilyich locked the door and began to look at himself in the mirror: from the front, then from the side. He took his photograph with his wife and compared it with what he saw in the mirror. The change was enormous. Then he bared his arms to the elbow, looked at them, pulled down his sleeves, sat down on the ottoman, and grew blacker than night.

“Don’t, don’t,” he said to himself; he jumped up, went to the desk, opened a case file and began to read it, but could not. He unlocked the door and went into the reception room. The door to the drawing room was shut. He went up to it on tiptoe and began to listen.
“No, you’re exaggerating,” Praskovya Fyodorovna was saying.
“Exaggerating? You can’t see it: he’s a dead man, look at his eyes. There’s no light in them. But what is wrong with him?”
“Nobody knows. Nikolayev” (that was another doctor) “said something, but I don’t know. Leshchetitsky” (that was the famous doctor) “said the opposite...”

Ivan Ilyich went away, went to his room, lay down and began to think: “The kidney, a floating kidney.” He remembered everything the doctors had told him, how it had come loose and how it floated. And by an effort of imagination he tried to catch this kidney and stop it, fasten it in place: so little was needed, it seemed to him. “No, I’ll go and see Pyotr Ivanovich again.” (That was the friend who had a friend who was a doctor.) He rang, ordered the horse to be harnessed, and got ready to go.
“Where are you going, Jean?” asked his wife, with a particularly sad and unusually kind expression.
This unusual kindness made him angry. He looked at her gloomily.
“I have to see Pyotr Ivanovich.”
He drove to his friend who had a friend who was a doctor. And with him to the doctor. He found him in and talked with him for a long time.
Going through the anatomical and physiological details of what, in the doctor’s opinion, was happening inside him, he understood everything.

There was a little something, a tiny little something in the appendix. It could all be put right. Strengthen the energy of one organ, weaken the activity of another, absorption would take place, and everything would come right. He was a little late for dinner. He dined, talked cheerfully, but for a long time could not bring himself to go to his room to work. At last he went to the study and at once sat down to work. He read case files and worked, but the awareness that he had an important, intimate matter put aside, which he would turn to when he had finished, did not leave him. When he had finished his work, he remembered that this intimate matter was his thoughts about the appendix. But he did not give himself up to them; he went to the drawing room for tea. There were guests; they talked, played the piano and sang; the examining magistrate was there, the desired fiancé for his daughter. Ivan Ilyich spent the evening, as Praskovya Fyodorovna remarked, more cheerfully than anyone, but he did not forget for a minute that he had important thoughts about the appendix put aside. At eleven o’clock he said goodnight and went to his room. Since his illness he had slept alone, in a little room next to the study. He went in, undressed and took up a novel by Zola, but did not read it; he thought. And in his imagination that longed-for correction of the appendix was taking place. Absorption, elimination, regular activity was restored. “Yes, that’s how it is,” he said to himself. “One only has to help nature.” He remembered his medicine, raised himself, took it, and lay on his back, listening to how beneficially the medicine was working and how it was destroying the pain. “Only take it regularly and avoid harmful influences; I already feel somewhat better, much better.” He began to feel his side: it did not hurt to the touch. “Yes, I really don’t feel it; it’s much better already.” He put out the candle and lay on his side... The appendix was correcting itself, absorbing. Suddenly he felt the familiar, old, dull, gnawing pain, stubborn, quiet, serious. In his mouth the same familiar foulness. His heart sank, his head swam. “My God, my God!” he said. “Again, again, and it will never stop.” And suddenly the matter appeared to him from quite another side. “The appendix? The kidney?” he said to himself. “It isn’t a question of the appendix or the kidney, but of life and... death. Yes, there was life, and now it is going, going, and I cannot hold it back. Yes. Why deceive myself? Isn’t it obvious to everyone but me that I am dying, and the only question is how many weeks, how many days... perhaps now. There was light, and now there is darkness. I was here, and now I am going there! Where?” A chill came over him; his breathing stopped. He heard only the beating of his heart.

“I shall not be, so what will there be? There will be nothing. Then where shall I be, when I am no more? Can this be death? No, I don’t want it.” He jumped up, tried to light the candle, fumbled with trembling hands, dropped the candle and candlestick on the floor, and fell back again on the pillow. “What for? It makes no difference,” he said to himself, staring into the darkness with open eyes. “Death. Yes, death. And none of them know, or want to know, and they don’t pity me. They are playing.” (He heard from far off, beyond the door, the swell of a voice and the ritornello of the accompaniment.) “It makes no difference to them, but they will die too. Fools. I go first, and they later; the same will happen to them. And they are enjoying themselves. Brutes!” Rage choked him. And he felt an agonising, unbearable heaviness. It cannot be that everyone is always condemned to this terrible fear. He sat up.

“Something isn’t right; I must calm down; I must think it all through from the beginning.” And so he began to think it through. “Yes, the beginning of the illness. I knocked my side, and I was just the same, that day and the next; it ached a little, then more, then the doctors, then the low spirits, the anguish, the doctors again; and all the while I was going nearer and nearer to the abyss. Less strength. Nearer, nearer. And now I have wasted away; there is no light in my eyes. And it is death, and I am thinking about the appendix. I am thinking about mending my insides, and this is death. Can it really be death?” Again the horror came over him; he panted, bent down, began to look for the matches, and pressed his elbow on the bedside table. It was in his way and hurt him; he grew angry with it, pressed on it harder in annoyance, and knocked it over. And, in despair, gasping for breath, he fell back, expecting death at that very moment.
The guests were leaving at this time. Praskovya Fyodorovna was seeing them off. She heard the crash and came in.
“What is it?”
“Nothing. I knocked it over by accident.”
She went out and brought a candle. He lay there, breathing heavily and very fast, like a man who has run a mile, and stared at her with fixed eyes.
“What is it, Jean?”
“No...thing. I knocked... it... over.” (“What is there to say? She won’t understand,” he thought.)
She certainly did not understand. She picked it up, lit the candle for him and hurried away: she had to see a guest off.
When she came back, he was lying the same way, on his back, looking up.
“What’s the matter? Are you worse?”
“Yes.”
She shook her head and sat for a while. “You know, Jean, I wonder whether we shouldn’t ask Leshchetitsky to come to the house.”
That meant calling in the famous doctor and not sparing the expense. He smiled venomously and said, “No.” She sat a little longer, then came over and kissed him on the forehead.
He hated her with all the strength of his soul while she was kissing him, and made an effort not to push her away.
“Goodnight. God willing, you’ll sleep.”
“Yes.”
## VI
Ivan Ilyich saw that he was dying, and he was in constant despair.
In the depths of his soul Ivan Ilyich knew that he was dying; but not only was he not used to it, he simply did not understand it, could not understand it at all.

The example of a syllogism he had learned in Kiesewetter’s logic: “Caius is a man, men are mortal, therefore Caius is mortal,” had seemed to him all his life to be true only of Caius, and certainly not of himself. That was Caius the man, man in general, and that was perfectly fair; but he was not Caius, and not man in general; he had always been a quite, quite special being, different from all others; he had been Vanya, with Mama and Papa, with Mitya and Volodya, with his toys, the coachman, his nanny, then with Katenka, with all the joys, griefs and raptures of childhood, boyhood and youth. Was it for Caius that there was the smell of that striped leather ball Vanya had loved so much? Was it Caius who had kissed his mother’s hand like that, and was it for Caius that the silk folds of his mother’s dress had rustled like that? Was it he who had rioted over the pies at the School of Law? Had Caius been in love like that? Could Caius preside over a session of the court like that?

And Caius really is mortal, and it is right for him to die; but for me, Vanya, Ivan Ilyich, with all my feelings and thoughts, for me it is a different matter. And it cannot be that I ought to die. That would be too terrible.
That is how he felt.

“If I were to die like Caius, I would have known it, an inner voice would have told me so; but there was nothing of the kind in me; and I and all my friends, we understood that it was not at all the same as with Caius. And now look at this!” he said to himself. “It cannot be. It cannot be, and yet it is. How can this be? How is one to understand it?”

And he could not understand it, and he tried to drive this thought away as false, incorrect and morbid, and to push it out with other, correct and healthy thoughts. But this thought, and not just a thought, but as it were a reality, came back again and stood before him.

And one after another he called up other thoughts in place of this one, in the hope of finding support in them. He tried to return to his former trains of thought, which had once screened the thought of death from him. But, strange to say, everything that had formerly screened, hidden and destroyed the awareness of death could no longer have that effect. Ivan Ilyich spent most of this last period in these attempts to restore the former trains of feeling that had screened death. Now he would say to himself: “I’ll take up my work; after all, I used to live by it.” And he would go to the court, driving away all doubts; he would enter into conversation with his colleagues and sit down, from old habit, absent-mindedly casting a thoughtful glance over the crowd and resting both his wasted hands on the arms of the oak chair, leaning towards a colleague as usual, moving the papers towards him, exchanging whispers; and then, suddenly raising his eyes and sitting up straight, he would pronounce the familiar words and open the proceedings. But suddenly, in the middle, the pain in his side, paying no attention whatever to the stage the case had reached, would begin its sucking work. Ivan Ilyich would listen to it, drive the thought of it away, but it went on with its work, and *it* would come and stand right in front of him and look at him, and he would be stunned, the fire would go out of his eyes, and he would begin to ask himself again: “Is it really the only truth?” And his colleagues and subordinates saw with surprise and regret that he, such a brilliant, subtle judge, was getting confused and making mistakes. He would shake himself, try to pull himself together, somehow bring the session to an end, and return home with the sad awareness that his work as a judge could no longer, as before, hide from him what he wanted hidden; that he could not escape *it* through his work. And what was worst of all was that *it* drew him to itself not so that he would do anything, but only so that he would look at it, straight into its eyes, look at it and, doing nothing, suffer unspeakably.

And to escape from this state, Ivan Ilyich looked for consolations, for other screens; and other screens appeared and for a short time seemed to save him, but at once, not so much collapsed as became transparent, as if *it* penetrated everything, and nothing could screen it.

In this last period it would happen that he went into the drawing room he had furnished: the drawing room where he had fallen, for which (how venomously funny it was to think of it) for the furnishing of which he had sacrificed his life, because he knew that his illness had begun with that bruise.
